reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest salivary gland neoplasm overall, most often arising in the superficial lobe and tail of the parotid as a painless, slow-growing, mobile mass.
Histologically biphasic and truly 'mixed': epithelial and myoepithelial cells set within a chondromyxoid or hyaline stroma, giving the classic myxoid appearance.
Driven in most cases by PLAG1 rearrangement (8q12) or, less often, HMGA2 (12q), frequently through gene fusions such as CTNNB1-PLAG1.
The capsule is characteristically incomplete with finger-like pseudopodia and satellite nodules, so simple enucleation predisposes to recurrence.
Recommended treatment is complete excision with a cuff of normal tissue (superficial or partial parotidectomy for parotid lesions) with facial nerve preservation.
Fine-needle aspiration cytology typically shows metachromatic fibrillary matrix with epithelial and myoepithelial cells; a hypercellular aspirate should not be over-called as malignant.
Long-standing tumours carry a rising risk of malignant transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, so a sudden change in a chronic lump is significant.
Deep-lobe or parapharyngeal lesions may present as a dumbbell-shaped mass with medial displacement of the tonsil and soft palate.
reference.pathophysiology: Pleomorphic adenoma arises from the terminal duct and myoepithelial cell compartment of salivary tissue and is characterised by both epithelial and mesenchymal-appearing differentiation from a common neoplastic clone. Recurrent chromosomal translocations activate the transcription factors PLAG1 or HMGA2, which reprogramme cellular growth and drive proliferation of ductal epithelial and modified myoepithelial cells. The neoplastic myoepithelial cells elaborate an abundant extracellular matrix that undergoes chondromyxoid, myxoid and occasionally osseous change, producing the tumour's distinctive heterogeneous stroma. Growth is expansile with a fibrous but frequently incomplete pseudocapsule, through which small tumour buds and satellite nodules extend, accounting for recurrence after incomplete removal and for the field of tumour left behind if the capsule is breached.
additionalInvestigations: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (with core biopsy where cytology is equivocal)
Ultrasound of the gland and neck as first-line imaging
MRI showing a well-defined, lobulated, markedly T2-hyperintense lesion
CT where bony involvement or deep-lobe extension is suspected
Assessment of facial nerve function before intervention
Histological examination of the excised specimen with margin assessment
redFlags: Sudden rapid growth or pain in a previously stable mass, suggesting malignant transformation
Fixation to skin or deep tissues or overlying skin ulceration
Rapidly enlarging long-standing tumour present for many years
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after adequate complete excision, with low recurrence when the capsule is respected. The principal long-term concern is malignant transformation, the risk of which rises with the duration the tumour has been present.
pitfalls: Enucleation or capsular breach with tumour spillage leading to multinodular recurrence that is difficult to eradicate
Over-interpreting a cellular aspirate as malignant on fine-needle aspiration cytology
Overlooking a deep-lobe or parapharyngeal component on clinical examination
Failing to recognise malignant transformation in a chronic, recently changed swelling
Inadequate facial nerve identification during parotid surgery
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Gnepp's Diagnostic Surgical Pathology of the Head and Neck
management: Undertake complete surgical excision with a cuff of normal tissue, performing superficial or partial parotidectomy for parotid lesions rather than simple enucleation to respect the incomplete pseudocapsule and satellite nodules
Identify and preserve the facial nerve during parotid surgery, assessing nerve function beforehand
Excise submandibular and minor salivary gland lesions completely with adequate margins
Avoid capsular rupture and tumour spillage intraoperatively, as this predisposes to multinodular recurrence
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy for recurrent, multifocal or incompletely excised disease
Maintain long-term surveillance for local recurrence and for malignant transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma
Refer to head and neck surgery for imaging, cytology and operative planning
